title: MedSIGHT: Unified Diagnosis and Grounding
one_liner: Medical vision-language models should answer questions AND point to the exact pixels proving the answer, not just one or the other.
lead: Medical image models face a split personality: some are trained to answer questions about what they see (comprehension), while others identify regions pixel-by-pixel (segmentation). But in real medicine, diagnosis comes first—a doctor says 'tumor'—then must show exactly where it is. MedSIGHT builds one model that does both, by teaching the language model to emit symbolic region codes that decode back to precise pixel masks, trained in three careful stages.

paras: Today's medical image models are split. Some are trained only to answer questions ('What do you see?') without marking regions. Others are trained only to segment (draw outlines around organs and tumors). A doctor using them has to choose: get a diagnosis, or get a marked-up image—not both.

The beginner's naive fix is to train one model on both tasks at once, feeding it all the mixed data. But it does not work: the model's visual understanding gets tangled. CLIP-based patch encoders (the standard vision backbone) extract only coarse, high-level features that discard the fine spatial detail needed for precise pixel-level grounding—they see 'there is a tumor somewhere in the lung' but lose the exact boundaries.

callout.html: Teach a model to diagnose OR to segment, but not both—and if you force both, the shared visual features are too coarse to ground the diagnosis on exact pixels.

panels.title: 1. The old split
panels.viz_args: Comprehension model: outputs text 'pneumonia' | Segmentation model: outputs mask pixels
panels.caption: Two separate models; doctor needs both systems.

panels.title: 2. Coarse vision patches
panels.caption: CLIP patches encode only high-level semantics, losing boundary detail.

panels.title: 3. Region Perceiver refines
panels.caption: Learns spatial structure on real segmentation examples first.

panels.title: 4. Codebook as language
panels.caption: LLM learns to output discrete region codes as symbolic anatomical labels.

panels.title: 5. End-to-end grounding
panels.caption: Model diagnoses AND decodes regions back to pixel-level masks simultaneously.

steps.text: Region Perceiver trains on medical segmentation examples to extract fine spatial features from image pixels.

steps.b: Step 2: Quantize regions into a codebook
steps.text: Assign each spatial feature (a list of numbers encoding location and shape) to the nearest discrete code; ensure codes decode back to correct masks.
Language model learns what each region code means by predicting text and reconstructing masks together.
Unfreeze only the LLM; let it learn to emit region codes and text in natural dialogue, grounding diagnosis to pixels.
Given a medical image and a question, model outputs diagnosis text and region codes; codes decode to exact pixel masks.

paras: MedSIGHT adds region-centric tokens—discrete symbolic codes the language model can learn to generate—so that diagnosis (text) can be grounded to exact pixel locations (masks). The standard baseline uses only high-level CLIP patches. MedSIGHT inserts a learned Region Perceiver that extracts fine spatial features, groups them into a codebook (a set of standard templates), and lets the language model treat region codes as vocabulary items, just like words.

hidden.name: accuracy of pixel-to-diagnosis alignment
paras: Every diagnostic statement ('this patient has pneumonia') only matters if the doctor can see which pixels prove it. Spatial grounding precision measures how well the model points to the exact pixels that match the diagnosis. In MedSIGHT, when the LLM emits a region code, that code decodes to a pixel mask; the precision is how well that mask overlaps the real anatomical boundary. High precision means no confusion—if the model says 'tumor here' and emits region code 42, decoding code 42 must reconstruct exactly where the tumor is. Low precision means the model names a diagnosis but the grounded mask is fuzzy or misaligned.

The paper measures grounding precision via intersection-over-union (IoU)—a standard metric comparing predicted and ground-truth segmentation masks. Each region code is pre-trained to decode to a specific spatial footprint; during joint tuning, the model learns which codes to emit to ground each diagnosis.

heat.caption: Darker codes have higher spatial-grounding recall (more often used by the model to ground real diagnoses).

reads.html: The Region Perceiver learns to recognize fine spatial patterns—where a lesion edge is sharp, where tissue is uniform. Its learned features (lists of numbers for each location) encode these spatial details. When quantized into codes, each code comes to stand for a characteristic spatial shape. The model's job is to learn: 'when the question asks about a tumor, emit the tumor-shaped codes and back them up with text.'

The paper uses IoU and the new DiagSeg metric (diagnostic reasoning + grounding together) to measure alignment. A high DiagSeg score means the model outputs the correct diagnosis AND the region codes it generates, when decoded, reconstruct the true segmentation mask.

mechanism.h2: Why grounding precision rises when you decouple learning
paras: The core problem: if you throw comprehension and segmentation data at a single CLIP backbone at once, the patches learn a muddled compromise—good enough for 'yes, there is a tumor' but too coarse to pin down 'here, exactly here.' The solution is to train in stages so each module specializes.

Stage 1 freezes the LLM and CLIP encoder and trains only the Region Perceiver on real segmentation masks. The Perceiver learns to extract spatial structure by being forced to predict masks; this creates spatial features (lists of numbers) that encode pixel-level detail. Stage 2 trains a codebook that maps these features to discrete codes, supervised by mask reconstruction—if a code does not decode to a sensible shape, it loses. Stage 3 unfreezes the LLM and trains text prediction together with mask decoding, so the language model learns which codes express which diagnoses. Because each module was pre-specialized, the final joint training is stable: the LLM does not have to reinvent spatial reasoning; it just learns to invoke the spatial codes that were already trained to ground its words.

stages.s: Region Perceiver refines patches into fine spatial features
Codebook quantizes spatial features into discrete region codes
LLM generates text diagnosis and region codes
Codebook decoder maps codes back to pixel masks

math.words: stage_1_loss = BCE_loss + Dice_loss (region perceiver learns mask prediction) | stage_2_loss = VQ_loss + L2_reconstruction + region_loss (codebook learns discrete codes that decode to masks) | stage_3_loss = LLM_loss + segmentation_loss (LLM jointly predicts text and generates region codes)
math.equation: L_total = w1 * (L_seg + L_ce) + w2 * (L_VQ + L_recon + L_R) + w3 * (L_LLM + L_seg)
symbols: Binary Cross-Entropy plus Dice loss (how well predicted masks match ground truth)
classification loss (predicting the anatomical class of each region)
vector quantization loss (how well each embedding maps to a codebook entry)
L2 reconstruction loss (how well decoded masks match the region embeddings)
region perceiver loss (preserving spatial grounding during codebook training)
language modeling loss (predicting the next word in the diagnosis)
stage weights (how much each stage contributes)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a tumor region has L_seg = 0.15 (pretty good mask match) and L_VQ = 0.05 (codebook vector is close to true embedding). Stage 1 contributes 0.15; Stage 2 contributes 0.05 + 0.08 (reconstruction) = 0.13. Small total means training is stable.

If we skipped pre-training and trained everything at once, the CLIP patches alone would struggle (L_seg = 0.35) and the codebook would have nothing good to quantize (L_VQ = 0.25). Total loss balloons and training destabilizes.

With progressive stages, each module solves its own job first. At Stage 3, L_LLM might be 0.20 (text prediction is harder), but the region codes are already aligned to masks, so the model can ground its diagnosis without fighting the spatial encoder.

math.note: Each stage independently optimizes its module; later stages inherit the earlier stage's learned features, so training is stable and each module specializes.

charts.title: Comprehension-only baseline
charts.note: Model answers questions well but has no way to show where the finding is.

charts.title: Segmentation-only baseline
charts.note: Model marks regions well but never explains what it is marking.

charts.title: MedSIGHT unified
charts.note: Unified training with staged alignment allows the model to diagnose and prove it simultaneously, because the Region Perceiver was pre-trained on segmentation so it already knows spatial patterns, the codebook was pre-trained to map patterns to interpretable codes, and the LLM only has to learn which codes and words go together—no reinventing spatial reasoning.

items.html: If Stage 2 (codebook training) is skipped or weak, the codes may not decode to clean masks. Then Stage 3 learning is doomed: the LLM learns to emit codes that sound right textually but fail to ground spatially. Solution: ensure Stage 2 has strong segmentation supervision.

If the Region Perceiver is not deep enough (too few refinement layers), it cannot overcome the patch-level bottleneck. The refined features remain coarse and spatial detail is lost. Solution: use sufficient Perceiver depth and ensure its pre-training includes fine-grained boundary annotations.

If Stage 3 unfreezes too much (e.g., the codebook vectors themselves), the codes can drift from their pre-trained spatial meanings. The codes become meaningless and grounding fails. Solution: freeze Region Perceiver and image encoder; tune only LLM, projectors, and codebook assignments (not vectors).

Stages are strictly ordered. Stage 1 produces spatial embeddings. Stage 2 produces codes that decode to correct masks (verified by IoU). Stage 3 teaches the LLM to emit those codes. The LLM never invents new spatial reasoning; it learns to invoke pre-trained grounding.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a minimal end-to-end demo: train a tiny Region Perceiver on a toy medical segmentation dataset (e.g., synthetic lung masks, 50 images), discretize regions into a small codebook (e.g., 16 codes), then train a small language model (e.g., 124 million learned weights, like GPT-2 size) on paired comprehension questions and region codes. Evaluate on a held-out test set.
demo.metric_eq: unified_score = (diagnosis_accuracy + segmentation_IoU) / 2; ideal = 100, baseline_split = 0 (one model solves diagnosis OR segmentation, not both)
demo.closing: The demo must show: the unified model outputs both text diagnosis and region codes simultaneously; codes decode to pixel masks that match the true regions; a split model (trained on only diagnosis) cannot emit region codes at all, while one trained on only segmentation cannot diagnose. Only the staged, unified approach achieves high unified_score.
